title: What are smart mobs?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a story about artist Ron English, whose building wrap for Ray-Ban was promoted with a staged "smart mob" of people in Ray-Ban sunglasses staring at it. This leads into an explanation of smart mobs (also called flash mobs): groups that assemble and disperse quickly using text messaging and cell phones, coined by futurist Howard Rheingold. They discuss protest tactics such as the Battle of Seattle WTO protests, surveillance as a counterweight to government power (citing citizen filming of a British hospital), the 2002 Miss World violence in Nigeria tied to text messaging, and playful smart mobs in New York, London, and Rome. They mention a Steve Martin bit about leading a club audience to McDonald's as an early example. The episode closes with a teaser and a plug for a How Stuff Works article on jet packs by Ed Grabianowski. Visa and Camry sponsor reads appear.

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor read
segments.summary: Hosts greet listeners and read a Visa sponsor spot, then open with a sad-news riff about artist Ron English.

segments.title: Ron English and the Ray-Ban smart mob
segments.summary: Ron English, described as the father of agitprop pop art, accepted money from Ray-Ban for a building wrap. Ray-Ban then paid a group to stand and stare at the wrap wearing Ray-Bans, which the hosts treat as co-opting underground culture.

segments.title: What smart mobs are
segments.summary: Smart mobs, also called flash mobs, are groups that assemble and disperse quickly, originally protesters, linked by cell phones and text messages. Hosts describe a central organizer sending directions and how this lets crowds stay ahead of police. The Battle of Seattle is mentioned as an early case.

segments.title: Surveillance, sousveillance, and citizen filming
segments.summary: The hosts contrast peaceful rallies that police can surround with mobs that scatter. They discuss surveillance and its opposite, with the Rodney King video as an example and a European group filming unsanitary British state hospitals and posting them online.

segments.title: Howard Rheingold, the term, and violence
segments.summary: The term smart mob was coined by futurist Howard Rheingold, who chose the word mob for its dark resonances. The hosts describe the 2002 Miss World pageant violence in Nigeria, where a newspaper article spread by text message contributed to deadly unrest, and argue that protest crowds can turn violent.

segments.title: Playful smart mobs and Steve Martin
segments.summary: Examples of performance-style smart mobs include a New York group bowing before a dinosaur at a toy store, a London group lying on furniture, and a Rome group asking a bookstore for nonexistent books. Steve Martin's stand-up bit leading a club audience to McDonald's is cited as an early precedent.
topics: New York toy store flash mob

segments.title: Consumer power and closing thoughts on smart mobs
segments.summary: The hosts reflect that consumers can wield power through such mobs, and joke about the fate of Ron English, Steve Martin, and smart mobs as sellouts.

segments.title: Jet pack article teaser, sign-off, and sponsor reads
segments.summary: Chuck reveals a How Stuff Works article on jet packs by Ed Grabianowski that reminds him of his childhood G.I. Joe jet pack. The hosts plug the website and the podcast email address, then a Camry ad closes the episode.
